Just so everyone knows, and can make an informed decision, Our place titanium pans do have a coating/layer on them that will flake off after extended use. It’s not as durable as they claim. They’re exploiting a narrow, technical definition of “coating” that regular consumers wouldn’t use. In cookware marketing, “no coating” usually just means no PTFE/Teflon—not that the pan is bare metal. There’s still a bonded surface treatment, but they call it “integrated” to dodge the word coating. It may be technically legal, but it’s clearly misleading.

When Kenji announced his partnership with Our Place, I looked into the Titanium pan and was very close to purchasing it. Before doing so, I decided to carry out my own research.

Since then, I have developed a number of concerns. The design of the lid appears to be flawed, and I am also uneasy about the unverified claims that the pan contains no “forever chemicals”. In particular, the proprietary non-stick coating technology used by Our Place has not, as far as I can determine, been independently verified by third parties. Similar claims previously made about Our Place’s enamel cookware have been questioned in multiple well-researched, scientifically grounded articles, which are readily available.

I want to be clear that I have a great deal of respect for Kenji and his work. I regularly watch his videos and own both of his cookbooks. My concern is that many people place a high level of trust in his recommendations, particularly when it comes to cookware, and may therefore purchase this pan without conducting their own research. If issues were to emerge in the future with the product or with Our Place as a company, those people may feel misled, which could ultimately reflect unfairly on Kenji himself. That possibility is what gives me pause about this partnership.

19:29 — Not trying to be a jerk, because I really am a long time loyal Kenji fan, but this testing methodology was absolutely misrepresentative about how these pans performed in the non-stick tests, and I kind think Kenji knows it deep down.  Kenji, your pan preheat temperatures for the cast iron and titanium pans were MUCH hotter than you did with the teflon.  Just look at how the egg reacts in those two pans: instant bubbling and spitting sounds, almost instant browning forming around the edges.  Meanwhile, the teflon pan was probably closer to 315º, and was barely starting to sputter after several seconds in the pan.  Look, I get that you can't use the control freak because the teflon pan isn't induction compatible, but you could have at least used an infrared thermometer before dropping in the eggs.  Because here's the thing, I can get those exact same sliding egg results even in a stainless steel skillet as long as the heat is as high as yours was for the titanium pan.  This isn't a real test of the pan's performance in relation to teflon as much as it's a demonstration about temperature control (which teflon famously does NOT require).  So I say redo these tests with the eggs again, but this time drop all of them in at much lower heat settings and temps (≈ 300-315º) and THEN see how well they perform compared to teflon.  

And don't get me wrong, I am not a teflon lover or something; I am a huge convert of the Strata carbon clad, and I understand that it will never be as idiot-proof as teflon pans and that I need to use cautious temperature management.   But I get really irritated when content creators oversell the properties of their new cookware with some gimmicky comparison that completely defeats the purpose of what they are trying to demonstrate.  If your pan is as good as you say, then cook it over a lower heat with more controlled variables.  Or even better, do a long and slow soft-scrambled egg without any starches or other boosters.  Or at least come out and be upfront and honest about the WHY behind the results you got.

And to those who would point out "bUT hE Made fReNcH oMeletTES iN The pANS!"  Yes, and he also (once again) used crazy high heat to compensate, which is why all of those eggs had insane amounts of browning for only cooking like 25-35 seconds.  Were they still edible and delicious?  Almost certainly, and I'm not complaining about the imperfections of the eggs; I am complaining about the misleading "demonstration" we are receiving, when in reality the only thing we are being shown is how heat-control affects sticking in pans.  Once again, you could do these exact same "French omelettes" in a stainless steel pan if you managed your heat the same way.  I'm actually kind of bummed, because I trust Kenji a lot and I was really hoping to see just how that pan actually performs with these tasks, and I'm feeling kind of cheated because he clearly used heat trickery to mask these real-world scenarios.  

So Kenji, I hope I am wrong, and that this pan can perform as well as you say.  But I would call on you to redo your demonstrations with a more controlled heat variables that actually focus on the weak points of these pans, instead of using heat settings in which any pan type could succeed.

I think people are slowly waking up from the old cast iron fever dream...cast iron is 100% romantic and 100% impractical relative to other alloys out there. Not to mention the wrist-snapping weight. Cooking with cast iron over a gas ring flame is the worst in terms of heat uniformity across the pan. It does well for baking or roasting in the oven where it can heat uniformly, and if you either a) heat it on an electric element that heats the entire surface of the pan or b) use an aluminum plate on a gas element to spread the heat source around.

My preferred pans/skillets are cast aluminum. They heat up quickly and uniformly, they're light, and with a little bit of oil/grease, they can be as non-stick as cast iron or carbon steel. The one downside with cast aluminum is that I wouldn't simmer anything acidic in them.

The lecithin and emulsifiers in the spray bake onto the surface at cooking temps and polymerize into a varnish-like film. It's not the Teflon failing; it's a layer of burnt-on spray residue sitting on top of it. Once that layer builds up, food sticks to that, not the pan underneath.

That's why a lot of nonstick manufacturers (Tefal, Scanpan, etc.) specifically tell you not to use cooking spray. A brush of oil, a paper towel wipe, or plain oil in a refillable mister avoids the problem entirely.  That being said, this dude is already doing it up wrong....  So, his tests are invalid. I'm a big fan of Kenji, but I can't get behind the Our Place Titanium Pro.  It's a bit of a gimick and a play on words.  It's the same concept as hexclad but instead of teflon in the hexagons it's a "titanium oxide" coating.  So it's NOT a layer of titanium, it's just a teflon alternative.  Because Titanium Oxide is still new, there hasn't been enough research on what happens when it is heated or peels off like Teflon, so we can't really say "titanium oxide is safe" it's more of a "we don't know yet".
I want to see the A/B for "5 year old Teflon pan vs daily-use Titanium Pro pan". Because that's the real question: is an old teflon pan stickier than an old Titanium Pro pan.
